p.title: A network analysis of committees in the U.S. House of Representatives
p.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)

ext.title: Network analysis of House committees
ext.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), vol. 102, no. 20, pp. 7057-7062 (published May 17, 2005; approved April 5, 2005). Classified Applied Mathematics; submitted via PNAS Track II.
ext.document_type: Journal article (empirical network analysis with descriptive statistics; no formal hypothesis test)
ext.coverage: Full text read in one pass (578 numbered lines, entire 28,559-char file): front matter, abstract, introduction, network construction, clustering, voting SVD, conclusions, Table 1, Table 2, Figs. 1-4 captions, and all 25 references. Annotation file 3d886caf1dac.json read in full: 33 items, all type Highlight, all by Paul Goff, all with empty note content. Metadata hint was correct in title, authors, year and venue; DOI and page range added from the text.
ext.research_question: Are U.S. House committee assignments random, or are important committees "stacked" with partisan members? Can network theory applied to committee interlocks (common membership), combined with roll-call SVD, reveal organizational structure and correlations with political positions without using outside political information?
ext.theory: No formal theory is tested. The introduction contrasts several political-science theories of committee assignment (qualitative and some quantitative; refs 1-6) and notes there is no consensus on how assignments are set or changed between Congresses. The authors draw an analogy to corporate board interlocks, where shared membership is linked to diffusion of political donations, investment strategies and stock-market effects (refs 9-18). Working assumption: a committee-pair connection's strength equals shared membership relative to chance, so structure can be read off the membership data alone.
ext.data: Sample: U.S. House of Representatives, 101st-108th Congresses (1989-2004), committee and subcommittee assignments (Clerk of the House site). Roll calls: 102nd-107th from Voteview; 101st from ICPSR. Units: Representatives (two-mode nodes) and committees/subcommittees (called "committees"). Detailed example is the 107th House (2001-2002): 444 Representatives including midterm replacements (432 used in the SVD ranking; 443 in the Poole-Rosenthal comparison), 990 roll-call votes (749 used in the Optimal Classification comparison after removing votes with under 0.5% minority), and 113 committees (19 standing plus subcommittees and select committees). The 108th Congress is mentioned only as "data not shown" (Homeland Security grew to 50 members). Intelligence committee has 20 members.
ext.method: 1) Build a two-mode Representative-by-committee assignment network. 2) Project onto a one-mode committee network; edge weight = "normalized interlock" = observed common members / expected common members if same-size committees were assigned independently at random from the House. Value 1 = chance, 2 = twice chance, 0 = no overlap. 3) Single-linkage hierarchical clustering on normalized interlocks; dendrogram (Fig. 2) read as levels. 4) Visualization by a variant of Kamada-Kawai spring embedding that uses link strengths (Fig. 1). 5) Voting matrix B (n Representatives x m votes; +1 yea, -1 nay, 0 absent/abstain); SVD gives leading eigenvectors u(k), v(k) and singular values; a rank-2 approximation (Eq. 3) is used. Partisan coordinate = eigenvector that tracks party; bipartisan = eigenvector that groups nearly everyone. 6) Extremism e_i = |p_i - mean p| on the partisan coordinate; committee extremism = mean over members; clusters averaged likewise. 7) Vote-outcome reconstruction: sum the rank-2 approximated votes per vote; positive = pass. 8) Compare individual-vote classification with Poole-Rosenthal Optimal Classification (107th only).
ext.identification: None. The design is descriptive. The random-assignment baseline in normalized interlock is the only null model; no significance test or randomization distribution is reported for any interlock value, extremism ranking, or SVD component. The conclusion that committees are "stacked" rests on departures from that baseline, not on an estimated test.
ext.scope: Population: all House members and committee assignments in the 101st-108th Congresses (1989-2004); detailed illustration uses the 107th House only. Institution: U.S. House; Senate, party leadership decisions and assignment rules are not modeled. Era: 1989-2004. Partisan control: Democrats 101st-103rd; Republicans 104th-108th (Table 1 lists leadership).

key_findings.finding: In the 107th House, the four Intelligence subcommittees and their parent committee form a tight clique. Their normalized interlocks fall in 14.4-26.6, far above chance, and the five nodes sit close together in the Fig. 1 layout.
key_findings.location: Networks of Committees, PNAS p. 7057; Fig. 1 caption p. 7058

key_findings.finding: Select Committee on Homeland Security (formed June 2002, nine members) is strongly tied to the 13-member Rules Committee, via two shared members. Its tie to the Legislative and Budget Process Subcommittee of Rules, via the same two members, is stronger still.
key_findings.numbers: Rules: normalized interlock 7.4 (2 common members); Legislative and Budget Process Subcommittee: 13.7 (same 2 members)

key_findings.finding: In the 108th Congress the Homeland Security Committee grew to 50 members but kept a close association with Rules. The paper reports this only as data not shown.
key_findings.numbers: 50 members; normalized interlock 4.1 from 6 common members

key_findings.finding: Homeland Security has only weak ties to the Intelligence Committee and none to its subcommittees, despite overlapping-jurisdiction expectations.
key_findings.location: Structure of the House, PNAS p. 7059
key_findings.numbers: 1 common member with Intelligence, normalized interlock 2.4; interlock 0 with all four Intelligence subcommittees

key_findings.finding: Single-linkage clustering of committee interlocks yields essentially four hierarchical levels (subcommittees, committees, groups of committees, entire House), with a possible weaker fifth level of subcommittee groups inside large standing committees.
key_findings.location: Structure of the House, PNAS p. 7059, Fig. 2 (dendrogram, 107th House)

key_findings.finding: A rank-2 SVD captures most of the 107th House voting structure. The leading eigenvector accounts for 45.3% and the second for 29.6% of the sum of squares of the voting matrix; the paper says no other eigenvector exceeds a bound it gives as 1.6% (inequality glyph lost in extraction).
key_findings.numbers: 45.3% + 29.6% = 74.9%; remaining eigenvectors reported at a small bound of 1.6%

key_findings.finding: The partisan coordinate is the first eigenvector in the 101st-105th Houses and the second in the 106th-107th Houses. The other (bipartisan) coordinate groups nearly all members together and tracks motions most of the House approves or disapproves together.
key_findings.location: Voting Patterns, PNAS p. 7060 (Fig. 3 caption and text)

key_findings.finding: The two-coordinate reconstruction predicts the outcome of 984 of 990 votes (99.4%). Excluding absences and abstentions it gets 975 of 990. Under the most conservative test, individual yea/nay signs are correct for 92.7% of votes and 939 (94.8%) vote outcomes are right. Always guessing pass gets 74.2% (735 of 990). Similar results hold for the 101st-106th Houses.
key_findings.numbers: 984/990 (99.4%); 975/990 excl. absences; 939 (94.8%) conservative; 92.7% individual votes; baseline 735 (74.2%)

key_findings.finding: Against Poole and Rosenthal's Optimal Classification on the 107th House, the SVD ranking classifies 92.7% of individual votes correctly (432 Representatives, all 990 roll calls). Optimal Classification classifies 92.8% (443 Representatives, 749 roll calls).
key_findings.location: Voting Patterns, Table 2 caption, PNAS p. 7060-7061
key_findings.numbers: SVD 92.7% vs OC 92.8%; 432 vs 443 Representatives; 990 vs 749 roll calls

key_findings.finding: By mean extremism, the Select Committee on Homeland Security ranks above all 19 standing committees and is 4th of 113 committees. Rules is the second most extreme standing committee (after Judiciary) and 18th of 113 overall. The Intelligence Committee and its four subcommittees rank among the 10 least extreme of 113.
key_findings.location: Voting Patterns, PNAS p. 7062 (Fig. 2 color coding)
key_findings.numbers: Homeland Security 4th of 113; Rules 18th of 113 (2nd of 19 standing); Intelligence + 4 subcommittees in bottom 10 of 113

key_findings.finding: Fig. 4 projects votes onto the two leading eigenvectors. Passed and failed measures separate cleanly. The authors read the four corners as broad bipartisan support, support mostly from the right (passed because Republicans held the majority), support mostly from the left (failed under Democratic minority), and near-universal opposition.
key_findings.location: Voting Patterns, PNAS p. 7060, Fig. 4 caption

key_findings.finding: Authors conclude that committee assignments are not random and that some committees are stacked, and that the interlock and voting analysis indicates the degree of departure from randomness. No statistic for that departure is reported.

limitations: Stated: the 108th Congress results are shown as data not shown.
Stated: the authors discuss only a few observations in detail and say a rich variety of other results can be derived from similar analyses.
Stated: the SVD reconstruction is imperfect (92.7% of individual yea/nay signs correct under the strictest measure; 94.8% of outcomes under the conservative test).
Stated: the partisan coordinate "corresponds closely" to party affiliation, not perfectly.
Stated: extremism is measured relative to the House mean, which is usually skewed slightly toward the majority party.
Stated: the Optimal Classification comparison is applied only to the 107th House.
Stated: the Fig. 1 layout is a variant of Kamada-Kawai, so spatial closeness is approximate.

Observation (not stated by the paper; the paper has no limitations section): no significance test or randomization null is reported for interlock values, clusters, or the stacking conclusion; the 'not random' claim is therefore descriptive. Single session emphasis (107th) and no analysis of assignment mechanisms, leadership, or seniority rules.

rel.summary_md:
Porter, Mucha, Newman and Warmbrand (PNAS 2005) build a two-mode network of House members and committees for the 101st-108th Congresses and project it onto committee pairs. Each edge is weighted by a "normalized interlock": the number of shared members divided by the number expected if committees of those sizes were filled at random. Single-linkage clustering then finds about four levels of structure: subcommittees, committees, groups of committees, and the whole House. Subcommittees of the same parent form tight cliques; the Intelligence cluster has interlocks of 14.4-26.6 times chance. A separate rank-2 SVD of the 107th House roll-call matrix (990 votes) splits into a bipartisan axis (45.3% of the sum of squares) and a partisan axis (29.6%). It reproduces 92.7% of individual votes, close to Poole-Rosenthal's Optimal Classification at 92.8%. Committees differ in partisan extremism: Rules is 2nd of the 19 standing committees, Select Homeland Security is 4th of all 113, and Intelligence and its subcommittees are among the 10 least extreme. The analysis is descriptive. No interlock, cluster or the "not random" conclusion has a significance test.

The paper bears on the built system in three places. (1) The committee pillar adds every subcommittee seat on top of the parent seat at one-sixth weight, and Porter shows subcommittee membership largely sits inside the parent committee's membership. (2) In the say-do gate, one recorded Yea on a final-passage vote can corroborate a Champion cell, yet the dominant structure in a roll-call matrix is near-unanimous bipartisan agreement. (3) Two components cite Porter for "community structure", but no code uses committee co-membership or a community partition. Melange has no committee co-membership layer; committees enter only as a scalar pillar. Porter's normalized interlock reweights each edge by size. That must not be carried over to cosponsor edges, because per-edge normalization of cosponsor edges was measured and REJECTED.

bearings.paper_claim: In the 107th House roll-call matrix (990 votes), the leading SVD component is the bipartisan coordinate. It groups nearly all members and tracks motions most of the House approves or rejects together, and it holds 45.3% of the sum of squares, against 29.6% for the partisan coordinate. Always guessing 'pass' is right on 735 of 990 votes (74.2%). The Poole-Rosenthal comparison drops votes with under 0.5% minority (749 of 990 kept).
bearings.paper_location: Voting Patterns, PNAS pp. 7059-7061, Eqs. 1-3, Fig. 3-4, Table 2 caption
bearings.system_side: Path V of the say-do gate counts a category as corroborated when a member's mean signed final-passage Yea/Nay lean is at least 0.5 with n >= 1. The producer sums direction x (Yea=+1/Nay=-1) over every admitted roll call in Congresses 117-119 and applies no filter on contestedness or minority share. One near-unanimous Yea can therefore keep a Champion/Defender cell. The same vote evidence feeds rank honors (votes 0.4) and the per-area grade (0.4 x votes).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The direction carries over: in any modern House roll-call matrix a large share of variance is broad bipartisan agreement, so an aligned Yea on a lopsided vote does little to tell members apart. The size does not carry over. 45.3% is for all 990 votes of the 107th House (2001-02), not the CU final-passage subset of the 117th-119th, and the partisan coordinate has grown since then. The share of lopsided votes in vote_category_lean.json is unmeasured, so this is a candidate check (minority share per roll call), not a finding. UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: Subcommittees of one parent committee form cliques with very high normalized interlock. The four Intelligence subcommittees and their parent fall in 14.4-26.6x chance. Single-linkage clustering puts subcommittees inside their parent committee at the lowest level of a roughly four-level hierarchy.
bearings.paper_location: Networks of Committees, PNAS p. 7057; Structure of the House, p. 7059; Fig. 1-2 (107th House)
bearings.system_side: Membership adds each subcommittee seat as BASE[tier] x 1/6 on top of the full-committee seat, and subcommittee leadership multiplies that seat weight again (Chair sub 7.5, Ranking 4.5). The 1/6 is owner judgment. Seats are treated as independent additive units of CU structural power.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Porter measures redundancy of membership, not influence. The finding says subcommittee seats are nested inside the parent, not separate exposures, so additive counting rewards members with many sub seats under one parent. Whether that matters for CU outcomes is untested. The data are the 107th House only; Senate assignment differs; Financial Services subcommittees are not singled out in the paper. Descriptive, no test.

bearings.paper_claim: Committee assignments are not random, and committees differ systematically in the mean partisan extremism of their members. Rules is 2nd of the 19 standing committees (18th of 113). Select Homeland Security is 4th of 113. Intelligence and its four subcommittees are in the 10 least extreme of 113.
bearings.paper_location: Voting Patterns, PNAS p. 7062; Fig. 2 color coding; Conclusions
bearings.system_side: The committee score depends only on CU-relevance tier and leadership role (BASE Highly 3.0 / Moderately 1.8 / Slightly 0.9). The party elite bonus is display-only. The pillar knows nothing about a committee's partisan composition or whether it is stacked.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies only if Paul wants committee seats read in light of composition: a seat on a stacked, extreme committee may signal party loyalty rather than CU leverage, which is his chicken-or-egg concern. The paper's extremism is relative to the House mean of the 107th Congress (Republican majority) and is never tied to policy outcomes. It is evidence of heterogeneity, not a weight to adopt.

bearings.paper_claim: Porter et al. find hierarchical clusters in a committee-committee co-membership network built from assignment data. They do not study cosponsorship or recruitment communities.
bearings.paper_location: Structure of the House, PNAS p. 7059, Fig. 2
bearings.system_side: The component record says it assumes 'community structure is exploitable (Porter-Mucha-Newman; Kim-Kunisky)'. The built budgetRecruit uses only GCOMB neighbour-locality coverage and a degree-pruning floor (DEG >= 0.1 x mean degree) on the cosponsor kernel. It uses no community partition and no committee data. The template comment cites Sotoudeh-Porter-Krishnagopal, not Porter 2005.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The citation does not ground what is built: there is a different network (committee interlock versus cosponsor kernel) and no community step in the code. The component listing's code path (fec/templates/) is also stale; the file lives at fec/surfaces/templates/.

bearings.paper_claim: A two-mode member x committee network, projected with an observed/expected-overlap weight (1 = chance), recovers House organizational structure from assignment data alone, with no political information.
bearings.system_side: load_network reads only the congress_cosponsor_network (or holistic and sector cosponsor families), mean-symmetrized. The multilayer build adds social and press layers. No committee co-membership layer exists anywhere in fec/network, so committees enter the system only as the scalar Influence pillar.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paul's annotation and his component position cite Porter as grounding for the cosponsor graph, but Porter's tie is committee co-membership, a different relation. A committee layer would be new and unvalidated. Its observed/expected weighting must stay on that new layer and must NOT be applied to cosponsor edges, where per-edge normalization was measured and REJECTED.

bearings.paper_claim: Raw shared membership is uninformative without a size baseline. Porter divides the observed common members by the count expected under random assignment of same-size committees, so large containers do not produce spuriously strong ties.
bearings.paper_location: Networks of Committees, PNAS p. 7057 (normalized interlock definition)
bearings.system_side: Staffer exposure integrates duration / max(1, n-1)^gamma over concurrent headcount, so larger offices dilute pairwise contact. This answers the recorded artifacts that staffer degree tracks largest office size (r = 0.87) and that admin containers carried 70.8% of pairs.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The principle carries over (container size inflates co-membership), but the unit differs. Porter normalizes container-container edges against a random-assignment null; the system dilutes person-person exposure by headcount. Porter offers no evidence that 1/n is the right functional form, and neither offers evidence that the result reflects closeness or access (D-025).

gaps_exposed: The system has no committee co-membership (two-mode member x committee) layer. Committees reach the engines only as a scalar pillar, so the hierarchy and cross-committee interlocks Porter documents never enter cascades or path-finding.

The roll-call vote evidence (vote_category_lean.json) has no contestedness or minority-share filter. Porter and Poole-Rosenthal show that near-unanimous votes dominate the roll-call matrix and should be screened out before votes are used to tell members apart (OC drops votes with under 0.5% minority).
The committee pillar ignores partisan composition and stacking, and treats subcommittee seats as additive even though Porter shows they nest within the parent.

Nothing in the system builds a member ideal-point or partisan/bipartisan coordinate from roll calls. Porter's SVD gets 92.7% individual-vote reproduction from two coordinates, which would be a cheap baseline for checking whether stance labels add anything beyond party or ideology on CU votes.
There is no random-assignment null for any co-membership edge (committee, caucus or staffer container) against which to judge whether a tie is above chance.
flags: Porter's normalized interlock (observed/expected shared members) is a per-edge size normalization. Per-edge normalization was measured and REJECTED for the cosponsor network (brain topics/2026-06-feature-cosponsor-and-sector-networks.md:101). Do not recommend porting it to cosponsor edges; at most it belongs on a new committee layer, UNVERIFIED.

Porter's SVD roll-call coordinates are a NOMINATE-class ideal-point method. Paul rejected DW-NOMINATE vote edges for the signed coalitions (same brain note, line 93). Do not re-propose SVD-derived vote edges.

Citation drift: melange-pathfinding.multi-target-and-budget-modes and melange-sna.cosponsor-network cite Porter et al. 2005 for community structure in a cosponsor graph, but the paper analyzes committee co-membership and the built code has no community partition. The Porter-lineage paper on cosponsorship is Sotoudeh-Porter-Krishnagopal 2024.

Committee 'extremism' and 'stacking' in Porter are descriptive, with no significance test or randomization null. Any wording that committees 'are stacked' should carry that label and its window (107th House, 113 committees).

The say-do bearing is a candidate check, not a measured defect. The share of lopsided votes behind Path V corroborations has not been computed; it stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's takeaways broadly match the paper (strong within-committee ties, a general hierarchy, and partisan alignment correlating with committee selection), with one misreading. He describes "a two-mode committee network and a one-mode representative network", but the paper projects the two-mode network onto a committee-to-committee network; representatives are not projected. His Weakness 1 (chicken-or-egg causality) is correct and stronger than he states: the paper has no identification and no significance test at all. His Weakness 2 (can members and committees share one graph?) is answered by the paper itself, since the two-mode assignment network is exactly that graph. His inferred system link, "multi-layer committee network for the present research", is stale against the built system. Melange has no committee co-membership layer; committees enter only as the Influence pillar scalar (committee_scores.py), and the components that cite Porter for community structure do not implement any. His committee-pillar position that "committees are the structural layer of the House" holds, but as built the pillar uses neither the interlock structure nor partisan composition.

related.why: Porter co-authored it. It moves from committee co-membership to a cosponsorship influence network for House bill passage, and it is the paper the dashboard template actually cites.
Porter benchmarks its rank-2 SVD against Poole-Rosenthal Optimal Classification (92.7% vs 92.8%). NOMINATE is the comparison ideal-point family Paul rejected for vote edges.
It models how committee assignments are made, which is the mechanism Porter leaves open when concluding assignments are not random (Paul's chicken-or-egg weakness).
Committee request data would separate member preference from leadership assignment, which Porter's descriptive stacking result cannot do.
It also builds networks from co-membership (intraparty caucuses), a two-mode institutional-membership projection like Porter's committee interlocks.
It also derives member structure from House roll-call voting, as a co-voting network centrality rather than an SVD of the vote matrix.
It also recovers House organizational structure from network data, by signed partitioning of collaboration instead of unsigned committee-interlock clustering.
It is cited alongside Porter as grounding for community structure in the path-finding component, so the two should be read together when checking that citation.

paul_entries.text:
Mason, Porter, and Peter Mucha. A Network Analysis of Committees in the U.S. House of Representatives | *PNAS*, 5 Apr. 2005, [www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0500191102](http://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0500191102).

This article, conducted by Professors Mason Porter, Peter Mucha, M.E. Newman, and Casey Warmbrand, examines the United States House of Representatives, and more specifically its subcommittees, through the lens of Social Network Analysis, revealing strong linkages within certain committees and a general hierarchical structure. The network consists of two nodes: a two-mode committee network and a one-mode representative network, with edges representing the common overlap between the two. The multi-layering of this social network is prevalent to the current research by directly outlining the entire ecosystem of the U.S House of Representatives on the committee level, and details of the correlations between the overall partisan alignment and committee selection. The main weaknesses are as follows: First for correlation between partisan alignment and committee selection, what came first, the chicken or the egg? Second, which pertains to the present research, is how to display both the members and the committees on the same graph and whether that can be done and/or is feasible.
